new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given anywhere in the only phonological description of the language. Ugare is described as a two-tone language (H, L; rising/falling contours when both land on one syllable; long vowels carry one tone or a contour), with automatic downstep after L within and across word boundaries and morphophonemic upstep. Noun stems (1-2 syllables) show four patterns H, L, HL, LH; verbs fall into a high-tone and a low-tone class with tense/aspect tone melodies. The words stress, accent and prominence do not occur in the manuscript.
new_statements.exceptions: None relevant to stress. Tone residue noted by the authors: floating-tone morphemes underlying noun morphophonemics and tense/aspect forms remain to be identified; some noun stems appear toneless (L in isolation, H after a H prefix).
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is described at the word level (noun stems with/without prefixes, verb forms) and across word boundaries (downstep). Nothing on phrase-level stress or intonation. Source is a 1994 SIL working paper explicitly labelled preliminary ('our knowledge is far from complete').
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes 'Ugare' (autonym; Ethnologue/Glottolog 'Mesaka', also Messaga, Iyon), ISO iyo, Glottolog mesa1245, spoken around Akwaya (Southwest Region, Cameroon) with speakers also in Benue State, Nigeria. No dialect is specified; the Cassettas' data come from their SIL Cameroon work up to 1994. Blench writes the name 'Ugarə'.

new_statements.quote: Ugare has two tones, high and low. These sometimes end up on the same syllable, producing a rising or falling tone. Ugare has a downstep after any low or floating low tone, and an upstep which occurs in high-low noun stems when a high tone prefix is added. Upstep is also quite common in the verb phrase, as will be seen later in the paper. We do not mark low tone in the orthography, but for clarity, every vowel will have a tone mark in this paper

new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the 8 pages (the only hits for 'emphasis' are pragmatic, not prosodic). The work describes Ugare as a two-tone language (H, L; rising/falling contours on one syllable; downstep and upstep) with tonal verb classes (high-tone vs low-tone stems) and tonal marking of tense/aspect/mood; every verb form is given as a surface pitch pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Both manuscripts describe the same variety: the Ugare/Binangeli people, called Messaka by outsiders, about 5,000 speakers, mostly in the Akwaya subdivision of Cameroon's Southwest Province with the rest in Benue and Taraba States of Nigeria and a settlement in Kumba; the Cassettas' fieldwork ran June 1992 to September 1994. The verb-system copy on rogerblench.info is an 8-page version, whereas Glottolog ref 75296 lists a 45-page item of the same title; the noun-class ms. is dated August 31, 1994 (the target citation gives 1994a).

new_statements.rule_in_words: No mention of stress, accent or prominence in the whole manuscript (a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned plus a full read of the phonology overview and the tone subsection). Ugare is presented as a two-tone language (H/L, contour tones from two tones on one syllable, downstep after L or floating L, upstep of H-L noun stems under a H prefix); noun stems fall into tone classes (H-L stems that upstep, L vs L-H stems, apparently toneless stems that surface L in isolation and H after a H prefix); noun classes split into high-tone and low-tone concord classes.
new_statements.identity_note: Both manuscripts describe the same variety: the Ugare/Binangeli people, called Messaka by outsiders, about 5,000 speakers, mostly in the Akwaya subdivision of Cameroon's Southwest Province with the rest in Benue and Taraba States of Nigeria and a settlement in Kumba; the Cassettas' fieldwork ran June 1992 to September 1994.
